ESE 3107 Study Pack

Solar Thermal Engineering. One-shot notes, then every shortlisted past-paper topic (2019-2023) with full answers, slide figures and worked numericals. Your place, theme and text size are remembered on this device.

24-hour priority list

You answer 3 of 4 questions in each part, so each part has its own list. Study down both lists until the green pass line: about 2 h for Part A and 3 h for Part B, which leaves time for sleep and a last read of the one-shot notes. Alternate between parts (A block 1, B block 1, A block 2 …) so neither is left short. Chance: how often the topic came up, newer papers weigh more (2023 ×5, 2022 ×4, 2021 ×3, 2020 ×2, 2019 ×1). Covered: share of that part's past-paper marks you have studied once you finish the row.

Retake tip: read the Concept Primer first (30 minutes). Most marks here are theory you can learn by heart: collectors (A5), radiation laws (A3), instruments and radiation components (A2), concentrators (B2) and applications (B4). For numericals, the sun-angle calculator covers A1 and the storage-tank and still calculators cover B3 and B4. FPC performance (B1) and radiation networks (A4) are the hardest: leave them for last.

One-shot notes: ESE 3107 Solar Thermal Engineering

Sun angles (A1)

δ = 23.45 sin[360(284 + n)/365]; ω = 15(ST − 12), morning −; cosθz = cosφcosδcosω + sinφsinδ; αs = 90 − θz; cosγs = (cosθzsinφ − sinδ)/(sinθzcosφ), sign of ω.

cosωs = −tanφtanδ; N = 2ωs/15 (derive from θz = 90°). ST = clock + 4(Lloc − 90) + E (Bangladesh). Air mass m = 1/cosθz; Gsc = 1367 W/m2.

Khulna Jan 18: δ −20.73, N 10.78 h. Khulna Mar 8, 11 AM: E −11.5 min ⇒ 10:47. Lat 45, Mar 5, 3 PM: sunrise 6:27, α 24.4°, γs 50.5°W, surface sunrise 7:22. Nirala: θ 21.4°, θz 39.0°, Rb 1.20 (use full cosθ formula).

Radiation and instruments (A2)

Extraterrestrial (outside atmosphere, beam only) vs terrestrial (beam + diffuse). KT = H/Ho; diffuse fraction Hd/H falls as KT rises (Liu-Jordan, Erbs).

IT = IbRb + Id(1 + cosβ)/2 + Iρg(1 − cosβ)/2; Rb = cosθ/cosθz; monthly H̄T = R̄H̄.

Pyranometer: thermopile under glass domes, global; shadow band ⇒ diffuse; beam = G − D. Pyrheliometer: collimator tube on tracker, DNI. Campbell-Stokes: glass sphere burns card, > 120 W/m2.

Radiation laws (A3)

Blackbody: absorbs all, max emitter, diffuse. Planck Ebλ = C1/[λ5(eC2/λT − 1)]; Eb = σT4; λmaxT = 2898 μm K. Gray: ε independent of λ. Kirchhoff: ε = α (enclosure equilibrium proof).

Eb = ∫∫I cosθ sinθ dθdφ = πIb. dω = dA cosθ/r2. 2023: Ebλ(3 μm, 600 K) = 520, ω = 4.09×10−4 sr, Q = 2.74×10−4 W.

View factors and networks (A4)

Reciprocity AiFij = AjFji; summation ΣF = 1; superposition; crossed strings F12 = (Σcrossed − Σuncrossed)/2L1. F1-3 = F1→(2,3) − F1-2. 2019: F12 0.075, F21 0.050; 2022: 0.075.

Surface R = (1 − ε)/Aε, space R = 1/AF. Plates q = σ(T14 − T24)/(1/ε1 + 1/ε2 − 1) ⇒ 13.9 kW/m2. Reradiating J = Eb. Triangle duct: −28 kW/m (remove). N shields: q/(N + 1).

Collectors (A5)

FPC (< 80 °C), ETC, CPC; trough, Fresnel (1-axis); dish, tower (2-axis). FPC: glazing, absorber (selective α 0.95, ε 0.1), risers + headers, insulation, casing. Greenhouse effect of glass.

ETC: vacuum kills convection/conduction ⇒ UL 1-2 vs 4-8 ⇒ flatter efficiency line, better hot/cold/windy. Heat pipe: boil low, condense in manifold, drip back; tilt ≥ 25°; freeze-proof, one-way.

FPC performance (B1)

Qu = AcFR[S − UL(Ti − Ta)]; η = FR(τα) − FRUL(Ti − Ta)/I. Ic = UL(Ti − Ta)/(τα). F′ (local fluid), FR (inlet fluid) = F′F″.

F′ = (1/UL)/{W[1/UL(D + (W − D)F) + 1/Cb + 1/πDihfi]}; F = tanh x/x, x = m(W − D)/2. UL = Ut + Ub + Ue; Hollands Nu; Tsky = Ta − 6.

2020: F 0.961, F′ 0.912, FR 0.868, Qu 2.10 kW, η 65.7%. 2021: Ut 3.39 + Ub 0.6 = 4.0. 2019: Ut 5.40, UL 6.23. 2022 dark test: 12.4.

Concentrators (B2)

C = Aa/Ar; acceptance 2θc; intercept γ. Cmax = 1/sin2θs = 46,747 (3-D), 1/sinθs = 216 (2-D), θs = 0.265°: from Tr ≤ Ts.

Tracking: beam only, small acceptance angle. Single-axis (E-W, N-S, polar) vs two-axis. Pros: high T, small loss area. Cons: no diffuse, tracking, cleaning. Reflector: high specular ρ, durable, cheap.

Water heating and storage (B3)

Passive: thermosiphon (tank ≥ 0.3 m above collector), ICS (night loss: selective coat, covers). Active: direct (open loop, differential thermostat), indirect (antifreeze + heat exchanger). Reverse circulation: height, check valve.

T+ = T + [Qu − L − UA(T − Ta)3600]/mcp. 2019: 45 → 86.4 °C. 2022: 40 → 116.9 °C (flag: above boiling, pressurised).

Applications (B4)

Dryers: direct (cabinet), indirect (collector + chamber + chimney), PV fans. Still: qew = 0.016273hcw(Pw − Pg), P = e25.317 − 5144/T Pa; 50/40 ⇒ 0.282 kg/m2h; 60/50 ⇒ 335 W/m2.

Desiccant wheel + heat wheel + evaporative cooler, regenerated at 60-90 °C. Absorption LiBr-water. Pond: 3 zones, salt gradient stops convection. Tower: heliostats, receiver, molten salt, turbine. Dish-Stirling 5-25 kW.

Definitions to write word for word

Solar constant: solar energy per unit time on a unit area normal to the rays at mean earth-sun distance outside the atmosphere, 1367 W/m2. Air mass: path length of the beam through the atmosphere relative to the vertical path, 1/cosθz. Hour angle: angular displacement of the sun east or west of the local meridian, 15°/h. Declination: angle of the sun at solar noon with the equatorial plane. Zenith angle: angle between the vertical and the sun line. Solar azimuth: angle from south to the horizontal projection of the sun line. Sunshine hour: time with beam irradiance > 120 W/m2.

Clearness index: ground radiation / extraterrestrial radiation on a horizontal surface. Diffuse fraction: diffuse / global. Geometric factor Rb: beam on tilted / beam on horizontal. Overall tilt factor: total on tilted / total on horizontal.

Radiosity: all radiation leaving a surface (emitted + reflected). Irradiation: all radiation arriving. Reradiating surface: adiabatic, net radiation zero, J = Eb. View factor: fraction of radiation leaving i that strikes j directly. Gray body: ε independent of wavelength.

Critical radiation level: irradiance at which gain = losses. F′: actual gain / gain with absorber at local fluid temperature. FR: actual gain / gain with whole absorber at inlet temperature. Aperture: opening receiving the sun. Acceptance angle: angular range accepted without moving. Concentration ratio: Aa/Ar. Intercept factor: fraction of focused beam hitting the receiver.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Collector families by temperature: FPC (stationary, < 100 °C) → ETC (stationary, 50–200 °C, vacuum kills convection and conduction loss) → concentrating (tracking, 100–2000 °C: CPC (compound parabolic collector), parabolic trough, Fresnel, dish, central tower).
  • FPC layers top to bottom: G-A-R-T-I-C: Glazing, Air gap, aRbsorber plate (selective black coating), Tubes (risers and headers), Insulation, Casing.
  • Heat pipe: liquid boils at the hot end (in the sun), vapour rises to the condenser at the top, gives heat to the manifold water, condenses and runs back by gravity. One-way, freeze-proof, a broken tube does not stop the system.
Before you start: what a solar collector is

A solar collector is a special heat exchanger that absorbs solar radiation, converts it into heat and transfers that heat to a fluid (water, antifreeze, air or oil) flowing through it. Unlike an ordinary heat exchanger, its energy comes from a distant radiant source with a low, variable flux (at most ~1000 W/m2), so radiation losses matter.

Classification (2022 4a, 2023 4a, 2019 4a)

Parabolic trough15-4560-400 °C

By temperature of application (Hasan sir): low temperature (< 100 °C: domestic hot water, pool heating, drying) — FPC, ETC; medium (100-400 °C: process heat, absorption cooling, small power) — ETC, CPC, trough, Fresnel; high (> 400 °C: electricity, furnaces) — dish, tower. Also by fluid (liquid or air) and glazed/unglazed.

Flat plate collector: construction and working (2020 3b, 2021 4a, 2022 4c, 2023 4b)
  1. Glazing (cover): one or two sheets of low-iron tempered glass (or plastic); transmits short-wave sunlight (τ ≈ 0.9) and is opaque to long-wave re-radiation; also cuts convection loss from the plate.
  2. Absorber plate: copper, aluminium or steel sheet, painted matte black or with a selective coating (black chrome, black nickel, TiNOX: α ≈ 0.95, ε ≈ 0.05-0.15); absorbs sunlight and conducts the heat to the tubes.
  3. Riser tubes and headers (manifolds): tubes bonded to the plate carry the fluid; the lower header distributes cold fluid, the upper header collects the hot fluid.
  4. Insulation: 25-75 mm of glass wool, mineral wool or polyurethane foam at the back and sides to cut conduction loss.
  5. Casing (container): aluminium or galvanised steel box with seals and gaskets; holds everything and keeps out dust and moisture.

Working: sunlight passes through the glass and is absorbed by the black plate, which heats up. Heat is conducted along the plate (fin) to the tubes and transferred by convection to the fluid, which leaves hotter (by pump or thermosiphon). The plate also loses heat: by radiation and natural convection to the glass and then to the sky and wind (top loss), and by conduction through the insulation (back and edge loss). The glass traps the long-wave radiation emitted by the plate (greenhouse effect). Useful heat = absorbed − losses.

Heat transfer mechanism (2019 4a): radiation: solar irradiation absorbed; long-wave emission from plate to glass and from glass to sky; conduction: within the plate to the tubes, through the tube wall and through the insulation; convection: from tube wall to the fluid (useful), natural convection in the air gap between plate and glass, and wind convection from the glass and casing (losses).

Glazing and absorber materials (2020 4b, 2022 4d, 2021 5b, 2023 4c)
ComponentRequired propertiesMaterials
Glazinghigh solar transmittance (0.3-3 μm), opaque to long wave, low iron, resistance to UV, hail, thermal shock; low reflectionlow-iron tempered glass (τ 0.85-0.91), anti-reflective glass; polycarbonate, acrylic, Tedlar films (cheaper, lighter, but degrade under UV and are partly transparent to long wave)
Absorberhigh α for sunlight, low ε for long wave (selective), high k, corrosion resistance, compatibility with the fluidcopper (k = 385), aluminium, steel; coatings: matte black paint (non-selective), black chrome, black nickel, sputtered cermet (TiNOX)
Insulationlow k, stable up to stagnation temperature (~200 °C), no outgassingglass wool, mineral wool, polyurethane foam (not at stagnation contact)
Casingstrong, light, weather-proofanodised aluminium, galvanised steel, fibreglass
Concentrating collectorreflector: high specular reflectance (0.85-0.95), durable; receiver: selective coating, high-temperature stable; cover: glass envelope (often evacuated)silvered low-iron glass mirrors, polished/anodised aluminium, silvered acrylic films; steel receiver tubes with cermet coating; borosilicate glass envelopes; thermal oil, molten salt, water/steam

Function of glazing: to transmit as much short-wave solar radiation as possible to the absorber while reducing upward heat loss: it blocks the long-wave radiation emitted by the hot plate and suppresses convection by wind; it also protects the absorber from dirt and weather.

Evacuated tube collector (2020 3c, 2019 4c)

An ETC is made of parallel double-walled glass tubes connected to a header. The space between the outer transparent glass tube and the inner tube (coated with a selective absorber) is evacuated (pressure < 10−3 Pa). Working: sunlight passes through the outer tube and is absorbed by the selective coating; the vacuum suppresses conduction and convection losses (like a thermos flask), so the heat goes to the fluid in or in contact with the inner tube (direct flow U-tube, or via a heat pipe). Because the tubes are round, they intercept the sun well over a wide range of angles.

Advantages and limitations of ETCs; why better than FPCs (2021 4b, 2019 5a, 2023 4d)
AdvantagesLimitations
Vacuum eliminates convection and conduction loss: UL ~1-2 W/m2K vs 4-8 for FPC, so high efficiency at large T − Ta (80-200 °C)More expensive per m2; glass tubes are fragile
Works in cold, windy and cloudy weather; useful all yearLower efficiency than an FPC at low temperature (less absorber area per gross area, gaps between tubes)
Round tubes collect well in the morning and evening (less incidence-angle loss)Snow does not melt off the front (little heat leaks out)
Tubes can be replaced individually; heat-pipe types are freeze- and scale-resistantCan overheat/stagnate at high temperature; vacuum may be lost over years
Lighter; can reach medium process-heat temperaturesHeat-pipe types need a minimum tilt (~25°)

Justification "ETCs perform better than FPCs": collector efficiency η = FR(τα) − FRUL(Ti − Ta)/I. Both have similar optical efficiency FR(τα), but the ETC’s vacuum makes UL 3-4 times smaller, so its efficiency line is much flatter: at (Ti − Ta)/I = 0.08 m2K/W an FPC may be at 25% while an ETC is still above 55%. This advantage is largest in winter, in wind and for hot-water/process temperatures; only for pool heating near ambient is an FPC as good or better.

Heat-pipe evacuated tube collector (2021 4c, 2022 4b, 2023 6b)
  1. Construction: each evacuated glass tube contains a flat or curved copper/aluminium absorber fin with a selective coating, bonded to a sealed copper heat pipe. The heat pipe is itself evacuated and holds a small quantity of a working liquid (water with additives, alcohol); its top end is a larger condenser bulb that plugs into a dry well in an insulated manifold (header) through which water or glycol flows.
  2. Working: the absorber heats the lower part of the heat pipe (evaporator); the low pressure lets the liquid boil at 25-30 °C; the vapour rises to the condenser bulb, gives up its latent heat to the manifold fluid and condenses; the condensate returns by gravity to the bottom. The cycle repeats as long as the sun shines (a passive, one-way "thermal diode": no reverse flow at night).
  3. Features: no water inside the glass tube (freeze-proof, no scale, a broken tube does not stop the system), dry connection allows tube replacement without draining, minimum tilt about 25° so the condensate can return.

Memory trick: FPC parts "G-A-T-H-I-C": Glazing, Absorber, Tubes, Headers, Insulation, Casing. ETC = "thermos flask for sunlight". Heat pipe = "boil low, condense high, drip back".

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Pyra-NO-meter sees the whole dome (global = beam + diffuse, thermopile under a glass dome; add a shadow band to get diffuse only, then beam = global − diffuse). Pyr-HELIO-meter stares at Helios (beam only, long collimating tube that tracks the sun).
  • Clearness index KT = H/Ho (ground / top of atmosphere). Clear day KT high → diffuse fraction Hd/H low. Cloudy: the opposite.
  • Tilted surface: IT = IbRb + Id(1 + cosβ)/2 + ρgI(1 − cosβ)/2: beam × geometric factor + sky it can see + ground it can see.
Before you start: what happens to sunlight on its way down

Outside the atmosphere the sun gives 1367 W/m2. In the atmosphere some is absorbed (ozone, water vapour, CO2), some is scattered (air molecules, dust, clouds). What reaches the ground arrives as beam (straight from the sun) and diffuse (scattered, from the whole sky). Their sum on a horizontal surface is the global radiation.

Units: irradiance G or I in W/m2 (a rate); irradiation H (per day) or I (per hour) in MJ/m2.

Extraterrestrial vs terrestrial radiation (2021 1c, 2023 1d, 2019 2b)
Extraterrestrial radiationTerrestrial radiation
Solar radiation outside the earth’s atmosphere (Gon = Gsc[1 + 0.033cos(360n/365)])Solar radiation reaching the earth’s surface after passing through the atmosphere
Only beam (no scattering); no atmosphere effectBeam + diffuse; reduced by absorption and scattering
Varies only with earth-sun distance (±3.3%) and geometry; predictableVaries with weather, clouds, pollution, air mass, altitude; must be measured
Spectrum close to a 5777 K blackbody (0.25-3 μm)Spectrum has absorption bands (O3 UV, H2O and CO2 infrared)
Used as the reference Ho for the clearness indexMeasured with pyranometers and pyrheliometers

Beam radiation: received directly from the sun’s disc without scattering. Diffuse: received after its direction has been changed by scattering. Global (total): beam + diffuse on a horizontal surface. Geometric factor Rb = cosθ/cosθz: ratio of beam radiation on a tilted surface to that on a horizontal surface.

Clearness index and diffuse fraction (2021 1e, 2019 2a, 2022 2a, 2023 2a)
  • Clearness index KT = H/Ho (daily), kT = I/Io (hourly), K̄T = H̄/H̄o (monthly average): fraction of extraterrestrial radiation that reaches the ground. Clear day 0.7-0.75, overcast < 0.3.
  • Diffuse fraction Hd/H: fraction of the global radiation that is diffuse.
  • Relation: a clear sky (high KT) lets the beam through, so the diffuse fraction is small; a cloudy sky (low KT) scatters almost everything, so the diffuse fraction approaches 1. Empirical correlations: Liu and Jordan Hd/H = 1.390 − 4.027KT + 5.531KT2 − 3.108KT3; Erbs (for ωs ≤ 81.4°) Hd/H = 1.0 − 0.2727KT + 2.4495KT2 − 11.9514KT3 + 9.3879KT4 for KT < 0.715 and 0.143 above. Procedure: measure H, compute Ho from geometry, KT = H/Ho, read Hd/H from the correlation, then Hd and Hb = H − Hd.

Monthly average hourly clearness index (2023 2d): k̄T = Ī/Īo, average over a month of the ratio of hourly global radiation to hourly extraterrestrial radiation for the same hour (Io from geometry). Overall tilt factor R = IT/I (or HT/H): ratio of total radiation on the tilted surface to that on a horizontal surface; R = (1 − Id/I)Rb + (Id/I)(1 + cosβ)/2 + ρg(1 − cosβ)/2.

Radiation on a tilted surface (2020 2a, 2021 2b, 2022 2b, 2023 3d)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
IT = IbRb + Id(1 + cosβ)/2 + Iρg(1 − cosβ)/2Isotropic-sky (Liu-Jordan) model: beam + sky diffuse + ground-reflected.
Rb = cosθ/cosθzGeometric factor converts horizontal beam to the tilted plane (projection of the same beam on two planes).
(1 + cosβ)/2 = view factor from the surface to the sky; (1 − cosβ)/2 = view factor to the groundA horizontal surface sees all sky; a vertical one half sky, half ground.
Beam with the geometric factor: measure/estimate Ib on the horizontal, compute cosθ for the surface and cosθz, then Ib,T = IbRbe.g. Rb = 1.20 at Nirala (A1).

Monthly average daily radiation on a tilted surface (Liu-Jordan, Klein): H̄T = R̄H̄, with R̄ = (1 − H̄d/H̄)R̄b + (H̄d/H̄)(1 + cosβ)/2 + ρg(1 − cosβ)/2. Steps: (1) H̄ from data, H̄o for the mean day of the month ⇒ K̄T; (2) H̄d/H̄ from a K̄T correlation; (3) for a south-facing surface R̄b = [cos(φ − β)cosδsinω′s + (π/180)ω′ssin(φ − β)sinδ]/[cosφcosδsinωs + (π/180)ωssinφsinδ], ω′s = min[ωs, cos−1(−tan(φ − β)tanδ)]; (4) multiply.

Measuring instruments (2020 1b, 2021 2a, 2019 1b, 2022 1c)

Pyranometer measures global (beam + diffuse) radiation on a plane from the whole hemisphere (2π sr). Working principle: a black (high-absorptance) sensing surface under one or two hemispherical glass domes is heated by sunlight; a thermopile (many thermocouples in series) has its hot junctions under the black surface and cold junctions under a white surface or the body; the temperature difference produces a voltage proportional to the irradiance (about 10 μV per W/m2). The glass domes pass 0.3-3 μm and protect the sensor from wind and long-wave exchange. Examples: Eppley PSP, Kipp & Zonen CM11.

Measuring beam radiation with a pyranometer (2021 2a): fit a shadow band (shading ring) or a tracking shading ball that blocks only the sun’s disc, so the pyranometer reads the diffuse radiation Id (corrected for the sky blocked by the band). A second, unshaded pyranometer gives the global I. Then beam on a horizontal surface Ib = I − Id, and direct normal beam Ibn = (I − Id)/cosθz.

Pyrheliometer measures the beam (direct normal) radiation. Working principle: a long collimating tube with a small opening (aperture angle about 5.7°) is pointed at the sun by a sun-tracker so that only radiation from the sun’s disc and a narrow ring around it reaches the black thermopile (or, in an absolute cavity pyrheliometer, a black cavity whose heating is compared with electrical heating) at the bottom of the tube. The output is proportional to the direct normal irradiance (DNI). Examples: Eppley NIP, Ångström compensation pyrheliometer.

Sunshine recorder (Campbell-Stokes): a 96 mm glass sphere focuses the sun on a card and burns a trace whenever the beam exceeds about 120 W/m2; the length of the burnt trace gives the sunshine hours. Modern versions use photodiodes.

Memory trick: "Pyra-NO-meter sees the whole dome; pyr-HELIO-meter stares at Helios" (the sun). KT up ⇒ diffuse fraction down. IT = beam × Rb + diffuse × (1 + cosβ)/2 + reflected × (1 − cosβ)/2.

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

Every hot body glows. A blackbody is the perfect absorber and emitter. Planck gives its full spectrum; Wien says the peak moves to shorter wavelengths as it gets hotter (λmaxT = 2897.8 μm K); Stefan-Boltzmann gives the total, Eb = σT4. This is why a collector works: sunlight (5800 K) arrives at about 0.5 μm and passes through glass; the hot plate (350 K) emits at about 8 μm and glass blocks it.

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: thermal radiation

Every body above 0 K emits electromagnetic radiation because of its temperature. Hot bodies emit more and at shorter wavelengths: the sun (5800 K) mostly 0.3-3 μm (short-wave), a collector plate (350 K) mostly 5-50 μm (long-wave). This difference is what makes glazing and selective surfaces work.

Absorptivity α + reflectivity ρ + transmissivity τ = 1 for any surface; opaque surface τ = 0.

Blackbody and its features (2020 2b, 2021 2c, 2022 2c, 2023 2b)

A blackbody is a perfect emitter and absorber of radiation. Features: (1) it absorbs all incident radiation, of every wavelength and direction (α = 1); (2) at a given temperature and wavelength no surface can emit more energy than a blackbody; (3) it is a diffuse emitter: the emitted intensity is the same in all directions; (4) its emission depends only on temperature. A small hole in a large isothermal cavity is the practical approximation.

Radiation laws (2019 2c, 2021 2c, 2022 2c)
  • Planck’s law: Ebλ(λ, T) = C1/[λ5(eC2/λT − 1)], C1 = 3.742×108 W μm4/m2, C2 = 1.439×104 μm K: emitted energy per unit wavelength.
  • Stefan-Boltzmann law: the total energy emitted by a blackbody per unit area and time is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature: Eb = σT4, σ = 5.67×10−8 W/m2K4. It is the area under the Planck curve: Eb = ∫0∞Ebλdλ. A real surface emits E = εσT4. Example: doubling T (K) multiplies the emission by 16.
  • Wien’s displacement law: the wavelength of maximum emission is inversely proportional to the temperature: λmaxT = 2897.8 μm K. Sun 5800 K ⇒ 0.50 μm (visible); plate at 350 K ⇒ 8.3 μm (infrared). Obtained by setting dEbλ/dλ = 0.
Gray body and Kirchhoff’s law (2019 2d, 2021 2d, 2022 3c)

Emissive power E: radiation energy emitted per unit area per unit time (W/m2). Emissivity ε = E/Eb at the same temperature (0 ≤ ε ≤ 1). A gray body has emissivity (and absorptivity) independent of wavelength; a diffuse surface has properties independent of direction. Radiosity J: total radiation leaving a surface (emitted + reflected) per unit area, J = εEb + ρG. Irradiation G: total radiation incident on a surface per unit area. Reradiating surface: an adiabatic surface with zero net radiation (it re-emits all it receives), so J = Eb.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Small body (area A, ε, α) inside a large isothermal enclosure at T, in thermal equilibriumKirchhoff’s thought experiment.
Irradiation on the body G = σT4 (blackbody cavity radiation)Inside an isothermal enclosure the radiation is blackbody radiation.
Equilibrium: absorbed = emitted ⇒ AασT4 = AεσT4No net heat flow at equal temperatures.
ε(T) = α(T)Kirchhoff’s law: at the same temperature, total hemispherical emissivity equals absorptivity; spectral form ελ = αλ holds always.

Consequence for collectors: a good absorber is a good emitter at the same wavelength. A selective surface exploits the wavelength separation: high α in 0.3-2.5 μm (sunlight), low ε beyond 3 μm (its own emission), e.g. black chrome α = 0.95, ε = 0.1.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Sun angles, from zero

Every solar numerical asks one thing: where is the sun in my sky right now, and how squarely does it hit my surface? Three numbers decide it.

  • Latitude φ: where you are (Khulna 22.8°N).
  • Declination δ: which season. The earth's axis is tilted 23.45°, so the sun's noon position moves north and south through the year: δ = 23.45 sin[360(284 + n)/365], n = day of the year. +23.45° on 21 June, −23.45° on 21 December, 0 at the equinoxes.
  • Hour angle ω: what time it is. The earth turns 15° per hour, so ω = 15(solar time − 12): − in the morning, + in the afternoon, 0 at solar noon.

From these: zenith angle cosθz = cosφcosδcosω + sinφsinδ; sunset hour angle cosωs = −tanφtanδ; day length N = 2ωs/15. For a tilted surface the long cosθ equation adds tilt β and surface azimuth γ (0 = facing south, west positive). Rb = cosθ/cosθz tells how much more beam radiation the tilted surface gets than flat ground.

Solar time is not clock time: correct for your longitude (4 minutes per degree away from the 90°E Bangladesh meridian) and for the equation of time E (the earth's orbit is elliptical).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: where the sun is

To know how much sunlight a surface receives, we must know the direction of the sun. Five angles do this: the latitude φ of the place, the declination δ (which season), the hour angle ω (what time of day), and for a tilted surface its slope β and azimuth γ.

Sign rules (Duffie & Beckman): north latitude +; ω = 0 at solar noon, morning −, afternoon +, 15° per hour; azimuth 0 facing south, east −, west +.

Definitions (2019 1a, 2020 1a, 2021 1b, 2022 1a, 2023 1a)
TermMeaning
Solar constant Gscenergy from the sun per unit time received on a unit area perpendicular to the rays at the mean earth-sun distance, outside the atmosphere: 1367 W/m2 (WMO; some books 1361)
Air mass mratio of the mass of atmosphere the beam passes through to the mass it would pass through if the sun were overhead: m = 1/cosθz (for θz < 70°). m = 0 outside the atmosphere, m = 1 sun at zenith, m = 1.5 is the standard test condition
Zenith angle θzangle between the vertical (zenith) and the line to the sun; cosθz = cosφcosδcosω + sinφsinδ
Solar altitude angle αsangle between the horizontal and the line to the sun; αs = 90° − θz
Solar azimuth angle γsangle between due south and the projection of the sun’s rays on the horizontal plane; east of south negative, west positive
Surface azimuth angle γangle between due south and the projection of the normal to the surface on the horizontal plane (same sign rule)
Hour angle ωangular displacement of the sun east or west of the local meridian because of the earth’s rotation at 15°/h: ω = 15(ST − 12); morning negative
Declination δangle between the sun-earth line and the equatorial plane at solar noon: δ = 23.45 sin[360(284 + n)/365]; +23.45° on June 21, −23.45° on December 21
Solar time STtime based on the apparent motion of the sun: solar noon is when the sun crosses the local meridian; differs from clock time by a longitude correction and the equation of time
Sunshine hourlength of time in a day during which direct (beam) solar irradiance exceeds 120 W/m2 (WMO); measured with a sunshine recorder. The maximum possible value is the day length N
Beam radiationsolar radiation received from the sun without being scattered by the atmosphere (direct radiation)
Irradiationincident energy per unit area on a surface, found by integrating irradiance over a time (J/m2): H per day, I per hour
Clearness index KTratio of radiation on a horizontal surface at the ground to the extraterrestrial radiation on a horizontal surface for the same period: KT = H/Ho

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Radiation networks, from zero

Radiation between real surfaces is solved just like an electric circuit. Each surface has a "battery" Eb = σT4. What actually leaves the surface is its radiosity J (emitted + reflected).

  • Surface resistance (1 − ε)/(Aε) between Eb and J: zero for a blackbody (ε = 1), so J = Eb.
  • Space resistance 1/(A1F12) between J1 and J2: how badly the surfaces see each other.

Two parallel plates: three resistances in series, giving q = σ(T14 − T24)/(1/ε1 + 1/ε2 − 1). A shield adds two more surface resistances and one more space resistance, so with N shields of the same ε the heat drops to 1/(N + 1). A reradiating (insulated) surface has J = Eb and zero net heat: it just bounces energy on.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: view factors and networks

Radiation exchange between surfaces depends on their temperatures, emissivities and how well they "see" each other. The view factor Fij is a purely geometric number: the fraction of radiation leaving surface i that strikes surface j directly. For gray diffuse surfaces the exchange is solved like an electric circuit with "potentials" Eb = σT4 and J.

View factor relations (2021 3a, 2019 3a, 2022 2d, 2023 3a)
  1. Reciprocity: AiFij = AjFji (follows from the double-integral definition, which is symmetric in i and j).
  2. Summation: in an enclosure of N surfaces, Σj=1N Fij = 1 (all radiation leaving i lands somewhere); Fii = 0 for a flat or convex surface.
  3. Superposition: Fi→(j,k) = Fij + Fik (but not the reverse without reciprocity).
  4. Symmetry: identical surfaces placed symmetrically with respect to i receive the same fraction.
  5. Crossed-strings method (Hottel) for long 2-D geometries: imagine strings stretched between the edges; F12 = [Σ(crossed strings) − Σ(uncrossed strings)]/(2 × string on surface 1). It works for any shape, even with partial obstructions.

Three-zone enclosure with a reradiating surface (2020 3a, 2022 3b)

A reradiating surface is well insulated (adiabatic) and has zero net radiation (Q3 = 0); it absorbs and re-emits everything, so J3 = Eb3 and its surface resistance carries no current. Its temperature is set by the other surfaces. Network: Eb1 — (1 − ε1)/A1ε1 — J1; J1–J2 through 1/A1F12 in parallel with the path J1–J3–J2 (1/A1F13 + 1/A2F23); then J2 — (1 − ε2)/A2ε2 — Eb2:

Q12 = (Eb1 − Eb2)/{{R1 + [A1F12 + 1/(1/A1F13 + 1/A2F23)]−1 + R2}}

Eb1 = σ6004 = 7348 W/m2; Eb2 = σ10004 = 56,700 W/m2; R1 = 0.3/0.7 = 0.4286
Space network: 1/A1F12 = 2 in parallel with (2 + 2) = 4 ⇒ Req = 1/(1/2 + 1/4) = 1.333
Q1 = (Eb1 − Eb2)/(R1 + Req) = (7348 − 56,700)/1.762 = −28,010 W
Q1 = −28.0 kW per metreNegative: the base receives 28 kW/m net radiation, so to keep it at 600 K this heat must be removed from the base (the question’s "supplied" means supplied to the base by radiation). Right wall settles at J3 = 38,026 W/m2 ⇒ T3 = 905 K.
Radiation shields (2021 3c, 2023 3b)

A radiation shield is a thin, highly reflective (low ε) sheet placed between two surfaces to reduce radiation heat transfer: it adds surface and space resistances. Uses: cryogenic vessels and multilayer insulation in spacecraft, thermocouple shields (to read true gas temperature), fire protection, furnace walls.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
N shields between plates 1 and 2: N + 1 gaps; all ε = 1 so each gap has only a space resistance 1/A (F = 1)Black shields: surface resistances vanish.
Steady: same q through every gap: q = σ(T14 − Ts14) = σ(Ts14 − Ts24) = ... = σ(TsN4 − T24)Shields neither generate nor store energy.
Add the N + 1 equations: (N + 1)q = σ(T14 − T24)Intermediate temperatures cancel.
qN shields = σ(T14 − T24)/(N + 1) = qno shield/(N + 1)The same result holds whenever all emissivities are equal (each gap has the same total resistance).

Memory trick: "Reciprocity, Summation, Superposition" (RSS). Surface R = (1 − ε)/Aε; space R = 1/AF. Plates: 1/ε1 + 1/ε2 − 1. Reradiating: J = Eb. N shields: ÷(N + 1).

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Solar still: sun heats shallow salty water → water evaporates → vapour condenses on the cooler sloped glass → fresh droplets run down to a channel. Salt stays behind. Output only 2–5 L/m² per day.
  • Solar pond: salt gradient (salty at the bottom) stops convection, so the bottom layer stores heat at 70–90 °C. Pool heating: just warms a pool, no gradient, no storage.
  • Solar power: trough (line focus, one-axis), tower (heliostats to a central receiver, two-axis), dish (point focus with Stirling engine). All feed a heat engine.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: using solar heat beyond hot water

Low-temperature solar heat (40-90 °C) dries crops, distils water, heats pools and drives desiccant/absorption coolers. High-temperature heat from concentrators (300-1000 °C) runs steam turbines or Stirling engines to make electricity. A salt-gradient solar pond is a collector and a store at once.

Solar crop drying (2022 8a, 2023 7c, 2021 7c, 2020 6a)

Solar crop drying removes moisture from agricultural products (grain, fruit, fish, spices) using solar-heated air to prevent spoilage and allow storage. Problems of open sun drying: contamination by dust, insects, birds and animals; re-wetting by rain and dew; overheating and loss of colour/vitamins by direct UV; slow, uneven drying and large space. How solar dryers overcome them: the crop is enclosed in a cabinet (clean, protected from rain and pests), drying air is heated in a collector (faster, controlled temperature), a chimney or fan gives airflow (uniform drying), and indirect dryers keep the crop out of direct sun (quality).

Direct (cabinet) dryerIndirect dryer
Crop in a glazed box: absorbs sunlight directly; air enters at the bottom, leaves through a vent at the topSeparate solar air heater warms the air, which flows (natural draught or fan) through trays of crop in an opaque drying chamber, then out of a chimney
Simple and cheap; small quantitiesBetter quality (no direct sun), better temperature control, larger capacity

Indirect dryer working procedure: ambient air enters the collector, is heated 10-30 K by the black absorber, rises into the drying chamber, passes over and through the trays, picks up moisture from the crop and leaves as warm humid air through the chimney; the chimney effect keeps the flow going. Advantages of solar drying: free energy, better hygiene and product quality, faster drying, less loss, higher market value. PV crop dryer (2023 8d): a solar air-heating dryer (collector + drying chamber + chimney) in which DC fans powered by a PV panel (with charge controller and small battery) force the air flow; the fan speed rises with sunshine, matching the heat supply, so the system works off-grid and dries faster and more uniformly than natural convection.

Solar distillation (desalination) (2019 8c, 2023 7d, 2021 8c)

Distillation is separating pure water from dissolved salts and impurities by evaporating it and condensing the vapour. Solar desalination uses solar energy to produce fresh water from saline or brackish water. Solar still working principle: a shallow basin with a black liner holds 2-10 cm of saline water under a sloping glass cover. Sunlight passes the glass and is absorbed by the water and liner; the water warms and evaporates; the vapour rises by natural convection and condenses on the cooler underside of the glass, releasing latent heat; the condensate runs down the slope into collection troughs and is drawn off as distillate. Salt stays in the basin and is flushed periodically. Output 2-5 L/m2 per day.

qew = 0.016273 hcw(Pw − Pg), P = exp[25.317 − 5144/(T + 273)] (Pa), ṁw = 3600 qew/λ (kg/m2h)

Numerical 1: hourly distillate (2021 8c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Pw = exp(25.317 − 5144/323) = 11,984 Pa; Pg = exp(25.317 − 5144/313) = 7,205 PaPartial vapour pressures at water (50 °C) and glass (40 °C).
qew = 0.016273 × 2.40 × (11,984 − 7,205) = 186.6 W/m2Dunkle’s evaporative heat transfer.
λ at 50 °C = 2382 kJ/kg (steam table)
ṁw = 186.6 × 3600/2.382×106 = 0.282 kg/m2h
Numerical 2: evaporative heat transfer (2020 6c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Pw(60 °C) = exp(25.317 − 5144/333) = 19,333 Pa; Pg(50 °C) = 11,984 Pa
qew = 0.016273 × 2.8 × (19,333 − 11,984) = 335 W/m2Heat carried by the evaporating water per m2 of still.
Distillate = 335 × 3600/2.358×106 = 0.51 kg/m2hλ at 60 °C = 2358 kJ/kg.

Note: C = 0.04 and n = 0.35 are the constants of Nu = C(Gr·Pr)n, used to calculate hcw; since hcw = 2.8 W/m2K is given, they are not needed (they would be used if hcw were not given).

Solar cooling (2021 7d, 2022 8b, 2023 8a)

Solid desiccant cooling (2021 7d): hot humid outside air passes through a slowly rotating desiccant wheel (silica gel or zeolite) which adsorbs its moisture (the air becomes dry and warm); a heat-recovery wheel cools it using the cooler return air; an evaporative cooler then adds a little water, cooling it further to a comfortable supply temperature. The wheel is regenerated (dried) by return air heated to 60-90 °C by solar air or water collectors. No CFC refrigerant; runs on low-grade heat; handles humidity separately.

Liquid desiccant cooling (2022 8b): a concentrated salt solution (LiCl, CaCl2, LiBr) is sprayed in an absorber/dehumidifier where it absorbs moisture from the supply air; the dry air is then cooled evaporatively. The diluted solution is pumped to a regenerator where solar-heated water or air (60-80 °C) evaporates the water and re-concentrates it; a solution heat exchanger saves heat; liquid desiccant can be stored (concentrated solution = energy storage).

Absorption cooling (2023 8a, any one process): LiBr-water machine: solar collectors (ETC, 80-95 °C) heat the generator, boiling water vapour out of the LiBr solution; vapour condenses in the condenser, passes an expansion valve and evaporates at low pressure in the evaporator, taking heat from chilled water (the cooling effect); the vapour is absorbed back into strong solution in the absorber, and a small pump returns the solution to the generator. The compressor is replaced by heat-driven absorption; COP 0.6-0.8.

Solar pool heating vs solar pond (2021 8a, 2023 8b, 2020 6a, 2019 8a)
Solar pool heatingSolar pond
Heats a swimming pool by circulating pool water (pool pump) through cheap unglazed plastic collectorsA large salt-water pond that is itself a collector and a long-term heat store
Low temperature rise (pool at 25-30 °C)Bottom brine reaches 70-90 °C
Collectors separate from the water body; pool cover reduces night lossesNo separate collector; salt gradient suppresses convection
Purpose: comfort, extends swimming seasonPurpose: process heat, desalination, power (organic Rankine cycle), space heating

Solar pond working principle: three layers: a thin fresh upper convective zone; a non-convective gradient zone where salt concentration (and density) increases with depth; a dense lower convective storage zone. Sunlight penetrates to the bottom and heats the brine. In an ordinary pond hot water would rise and lose its heat at the surface, but here the hot bottom brine is so salty that it stays denser than the cooler water above, so convection is suppressed; the gradient zone acts as transparent insulation (heat can leave only by slow conduction). Heat is extracted by pumping hot brine through a heat exchanger. Area-intensive but cheap, with seasonal storage.

Solar pool heating and direct dryer (2020 6a)

Solar pool heating system: the pool filter pump draws water through the filter and then through unglazed black polypropylene collectors on the roof; a diverter valve (manual or automatic) sends water through the collectors only when they are warmer than the pool; warmed water returns to the pool; a pool blanket at night cuts evaporation loss. A direct solar dryer is a glazed, black-lined cabinet in which the crop on trays absorbs sunlight directly; air enters through holes at the bottom, is warmed, removes moisture and leaves through vents at the top.

Solar thermal power: central receiver, dish (2020 6b, 2022 8c, 2023 8c, 2019 8b, 2021 8b)

Solar thermal power system: concentrating collectors convert sunlight into high-temperature heat that drives a heat engine (Rankine steam cycle, Brayton gas turbine or Stirling engine) to generate electricity. Collectors used: parabolic trough (most plants, 390 °C oil), linear Fresnel, central receiver with heliostats (565 °C molten salt), parabolic dish (Stirling, 750 °C).

Central receiver (power tower): a field of hundreds to thousands of heliostats (flat, two-axis tracking mirrors) reflects beam radiation onto a receiver at the top of a tall tower (C = 300-1500). The receiver heats a working fluid (molten nitrate salt, water/steam or air) to 500-1000 °C. Hot salt is stored in a hot tank; when power is needed it passes through a steam generator, and the steam drives a turbine-generator; the cooled salt returns to the cold tank. Storage lets the plant run after sunset. Example: Gemasolar (Spain), Crescent Dunes (USA).

Parabolic dish system: a paraboloid dish (or many mirror facets on a dish frame) tracks the sun on two axes and focuses beam radiation onto a receiver at its focal point (C = 500-3000), reaching 750 °C or more. A Stirling engine (or small gas turbine) mounted at the focus converts the heat directly into mechanical work, and an attached generator produces 5-25 kW. Highest solar-to-electric efficiency (~30%), modular, but costly and no simple storage.

Memory trick: "Dry, Distil, Desiccant, Dish". Still: qew = 0.016273 hcwΔP, ÷λ. Pond: "salt makes hot water heavy, so it stays down". Tower = heliostats + receiver + salt tanks + steam turbine.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Concentration ratio C = aperture area / absorber area. Maximum possible (sun's half-angle θs = 0.27°): 3-D (circular) Cmax = 1/sin²θs ≈ 45,000–46,700; 2-D (linear) = 1/sinθs ≈ 212.
  • Higher C → smaller hot receiver → less loss → higher temperature: CPC (compound parabolic collector) 1–10 (< 150 °C), trough 15–45 (to 400 °C), dish 100–1000, tower 300–1500 (to 2000 °C).
  • Concentrators use only beam radiation, so they must track the sun: one-axis for troughs, two-axis for dishes and heliostats.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: why concentrate

Heat loss is proportional to the absorber area. A concentrator collects sunlight on a large aperture (mirror or lens) and focuses it onto a small receiver, so the loss area is small and the receiver gets much hotter. The price: only beam radiation can be focused, so the collector must track the sun.

Definitions (2019 6a, 2022 6b, 2021 6a, 2023 5a)
TermMeaning
Aperture area Aathe plane opening of the concentrator through which the solar radiation enters (the projected area of the reflector or lens facing the sun)
Absorber (receiver) area Arthe area of the receiver that absorbs the concentrated radiation and delivers heat to the fluid
Concentration ratio Cgeometric: C = Aa/Ar; optical: ratio of average flux on the receiver to the flux on the aperture
Acceptance angle 2θcthe angular range within which radiation entering the aperture reaches the receiver without moving the collector; θc = semi (half) acceptance angle. Large 2θc ⇒ only seasonal adjustment; small ⇒ continuous tracking
Intercept factor γfraction of the reflected (focused) beam radiation that actually falls on the receiver; depends on receiver size, mirror errors and tracking errors; typically 0.9-0.97
Optical efficiency ηofraction of beam radiation on the aperture that is absorbed by the receiver: ηo = ρταγ[(1 − Aftanθ)cosθ]
Classification of concentrators (2021 6b, 2023 5c)
  1. By focus: line focus (2-D, cylindrical): parabolic trough collector (PTC), linear Fresnel reflector (LFR), cylindrical lens; point focus (3-D): parabolic dish, heliostat field + central receiver (tower), circular Fresnel lens.
  2. By optics: reflecting (mirrors) or refracting (Fresnel lenses); imaging (forms an image of the sun: trough, dish) or non-imaging (CPC: collects all radiation within the acceptance angle, no image).
  3. By tracking: stationary (CPC with large acceptance angle, flat plate with booster reflectors), single-axis tracking (trough, LFR), two-axis tracking (dish, heliostats).
  4. By receiver: flat, cylindrical (tube, often in an evacuated glass envelope), cavity.
Concentration ratio and receiver temperature (2022 6c, 2023 5b)

A receiver at temperature Tr absorbs CηoIb per unit receiver area and loses UL(Tr − Ta) + εσTr4; the higher C, the higher the temperature at which gain still exceeds losses (Rabl’s diagram: the upper limit is the stagnation temperature, practical operation at 40-60% collection efficiency). Practical ranges: FPC (flat plate collector) C = 1 (< 80 °C); CPC 1-5 (to ~240 °C); linear Fresnel 10-40 and trough 15-45 (to 400 °C); dish 100-1000 (to 1500 °C); tower 100-1500 (to 2000 °C).

Maximum possible concentration ratio (2019 6d)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Sun: radius r, temperature Ts, distance R; half-angle θs with sinθs = r/RGeometry.
Radiation from the sun reaching the aperture: Qs→a = Aa(r2/R2)σTs4 = Aasin2θs σTs4Sun emits 4πr2σTs4, spread over a sphere of radius R.
Perfect (black) receiver radiates ArσTr4, of which a fraction Fr-s reaches the sun: Qr→s = ArσTr4Fr-sNo losses other than radiation back to the sun.
Second law: Tr cannot exceed Ts; at the limit Tr = Ts and Qs→a = Qr→s ⇒ Aa/Ar = Fr-s/sin2θs
Fr-s ≤ 1 ⇒ Cmax,3D = 1/sin2θs (circular), and for a linear concentrator Cmax,2D = 1/sinθs
Sun’s half-angle θs ≈ 16′ (0.265°): Cmax = 1/sin2(0.265°) = 46,747 (circular); 1/sin(0.265°) = 216 (linear)With θs rounded to 0.267° the value is 46,165; the course notes quote 46,747 (Kalogirou).
Tracking (2021 6c, 2019 6c, 2023 6c, 2020 5a)

Why tracking is necessary: a concentrator can focus only beam radiation that arrives within its small acceptance angle; as the sun moves (15°/h east-west and seasonally north-south), the focus would leave the receiver. Tracking keeps the aperture facing the sun so the image stays on the receiver; it also maximises the beam radiation collected (cosθ ≈ 1).

Single-axis trackingTwo-axis tracking
Rotation about one axis; follows the sun in one direction onlyRotation about two perpendicular axes (azimuth-elevation or polar-declination); follows the sun exactly (θ = 0 always)
Modes: horizontal E-W axis (adjust daily for altitude), horizontal N-S axis (tracks E-W during the day), polar axis parallel to the earth’s axis (15°/h)Used for point-focus systems: dishes, heliostats (each mirror), high-concentration PV (photovoltaic)
Simpler, cheaper, more reliable; for line-focus troughs and FresnelMore complex and costly, higher maintenance; collects the most energy (~35-40% more than fixed)

The question’s "three-axis" tracking is not a standard type; it is treated as single-axis vs two-axis. Tracking drives: mechanical/clock drives, microprocessor + sun-position algorithm (open loop), or light sensors with shadow bands (closed loop).

Advantages and disadvantages of concentrating collectors (2019 6b, 2023 5d, 2021 6c)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
Higher fluid temperatures (to 400-1500 °C): power generation and process heat; better thermodynamic (Carnot) qualityCollect only beam radiation: useless on cloudy/hazy days, poor in humid climates
Small receiver area ⇒ smaller heat losses ⇒ higher efficiency at a given temperatureNeed tracking systems: cost, power and maintenance
Reflectors are cheaper per m2 than absorbers; less expensive receiver materialReflecting surfaces lose reflectance with dust/ageing; need cleaning and refurbishment
Smaller heat-capacity mass ⇒ faster start-up; selective coatings/vacuum economical on small receiversNon-uniform flux on the receiver; high temperatures cause material problems

Materials (2019 6c, 2023 4c): reflectors: back-silvered low-iron glass, polished or anodised aluminium (Alanod), silvered acrylic/polymer films; receivers: stainless or carbon steel tubes with cermet selective coatings in evacuated borosilicate glass envelopes; heat transfer fluids: synthetic oil, molten nitrate salt, water/steam; structures: galvanised steel. A good reflector (2022 6d) must have: high specular (mirror-like) reflectance over the solar spectrum (> 0.9); accurate shape; resistance to weather, UV, abrasion and corrosion; low soiling and easy cleaning; light weight, rigidity and low cost; long life.

Memory trick: "C = Aa/Ar; Cmax = 1/sin2θs ≈ 46,747". Line focus (trough, Fresnel) = 1 axis; point focus (dish, tower) = 2 axes. Concentrators: "hot, small, but blind to diffuse".

  • Tank energy balance each hour: new T = old T + [Qu − L − UA(T − Troom)Δt]/(mcp). Losses use the temperature at the start of the hour.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: solar water heaters

A solar water heater = collector + storage tank + a way to move water between them. If the water moves by itself (density difference), the system is passive; if a pump and controller move it, the system is active. Domestic hot water needs only 45-60 °C, so flat plate or evacuated tube collectors are used.

Classification (2020 5b, 2019 7a)
  1. Passive: thermosiphon (natural circulation); integrated collector storage (ICS, batch heater).
  2. Active: direct circulation (open loop), indirect circulation (closed loop, heat exchanger), drain-back, air-water systems, heat-pump systems.
  3. Applications (2019 7a): domestic hot water for homes, hotels, hospitals, hostels; swimming-pool heating; space heating; industrial process heat (dairies, textiles, food); pre-heating boiler feed water; laundries.
Thermosiphon system (2020 5b, 2019 7b)

The storage tank is placed above the collector. Water in the collector absorbs heat, becomes lighter and rises through the upper pipe into the top of the tank; cooler, denser water from the bottom of the tank sinks through the lower pipe into the collector inlet. This natural (thermosiphon) circulation continues while the sun shines; the flow rate increases with the sunshine, so it is self-regulating. Hot water is drawn from the top of the tank and replaced by mains water at the bottom. An auxiliary electric heater near the top of the tank covers cloudy days. No pump or controller is needed.

Advantages and disadvantages of passive systems (2022 7b) and reverse circulation (2022 7c)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
No pump, no controller, no electricity; works during power cutsTank must be above the collector: heavy load on the roof, poor appearance
Simple, cheap, reliable, long life, low maintenanceLow flow; performance depends on stratification and pipe layout; less flexible design
Self-regulating flowFreezing risk in cold climates (open systems); scaling with hard water
Reverse circulation at night cools the tank; ICS has high night losses

Preventing reverse circulation: at night the collector cools below the tank (sky radiation), and the flow can reverse, cooling the stored water. Remedies: place the bottom of the tank at least 0.3 m (often 0.3-0.6 m) above the top of the collector; fit a non-return (check) valve or thermosiphon restrictor in the circuit; use a heat-pipe collector (one-way heat flow); in active systems, the controller stops the pump and a check valve prevents back-flow.

Direct and indirect active systems (2021 7a, 2023 7a)

Direct (open loop): a pump circulates the potable water itself from the bottom of the tank through the collectors and back to the tank. A differential thermostat switches the pump on when the collector outlet is about 5-10 K hotter than the tank bottom and off when the difference drops to 1-2 K; a check valve stops night reverse flow. Simple and efficient (no heat-exchanger loss) but only suitable where there is no freezing and the water is soft.

Indirect (closed loop): a separate collector loop filled with antifreeze (water-propylene glycol) or another fluid is pumped through the collectors and through a heat exchanger (coil inside the tank or external). The heat passes to the potable water without mixing. An expansion tank and pressure-relief valve protect the closed loop. Used in freezing climates and with hard water; slightly lower efficiency due to the heat exchanger.

Integrated collector storage (2021 7b, 2023 7b)

In an ICS system the storage tank itself is the absorber: one or more black-painted (or selectively coated) tanks sit inside an insulated box with a glazed top; water is heated in place; hot water is drawn from the top and cold water enters at the bottom. Problems: large tank surface loses heat to the surroundings, especially at night and in cold weather (the main drawback); water may freeze; little stratification; heavy. Solutions: selective coating on the tank, double glazing or transparent insulation, insulated night covers (manual or automatic), placing tanks in a CPC (compound parabolic collector)/involute reflector cavity, using the system for daytime loads, or adding a separate insulated storage tank.

Solar heat pump systems (2022 7a)

Water heating: a refrigerant circuit where the evaporator is the solar collector (direct-expansion, unglazed or glazed) or receives heat from solar-heated water; the compressor raises the temperature, and the condenser coil heats the storage tank. Solar input raises the evaporator temperature, so the COP (3-6) is higher than with an air-source heat pump. Space heating: collectors heat a storage tank; when the tank is warm enough (> ~25 °C) it heats the house directly; when it is too cool, a water-to-air heat pump uses the tank as its heat source (series system); a parallel system uses solar directly and an air-source heat pump as backup; dual-source systems choose the better source.

Storage: why and how (2019 7c, 2020 5c)

Solar input and demand do not coincide (sun at noon, hot-water demand morning and evening, none at night or on cloudy days), so energy must be stored. A storage system smooths supply, raises the solar fraction and lets the collector run at a lower temperature. How it works: during sunshine the collector loop delivers Qu to the tank (sensible heat in water, rock bed for air systems, or latent heat in phase-change material); the load draws heat; the tank loses UA(Ts − Ta) to its surroundings. Well-stratified tanks (hot at the top, cold at the bottom) return the coldest water to the collector and supply the hottest water to the load, improving performance.

Ts+ = Ts + (Δt/mcp)[Qu − L − (UA)(Ts − Ta)] (fully mixed tank, explicit hour-by-hour)

Numerical 1: 500 kg tank, 10 hours from 5 AM (2019 7c)

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
F′ and FR, from zero

The ideal collector would be at the temperature of the incoming water everywhere, so it would lose the least heat. Reality has two penalties, each written as a factor below 1:

  • Fin efficiency F: the plate between tubes is a fin, hotter in the middle than at the tube, F = tanh[m(W − D)/2]/[m(W − D)/2], m = √(UL/kδ).
  • Collector efficiency factor F′: the plate is hotter than the fluid next to it (fin + tube wall + inside film resistances). F′ = useful gain / gain if the plate were at the local fluid temperature.
  • Heat removal factor FR: the fluid also warms up as it flows. FR = useful gain / gain if the whole plate were at the inlet temperature. FR = F′F″, with flow factor F″ from ṁcp.

Then the Hottel-Whillier-Bliss equation: Qu = AcFR[S − UL(Ti − Ta)], S = (τα)IT. The critical radiation level is the IT where Qu = 0: Ic = UL(Ti − Ta)/(τα).

Before you start: the collector energy balance

Of the sunlight IT falling on the collector, a fraction (τα) is absorbed: S = (τα)IT. Part of it is lost because the plate is hotter than the air: UL(Tp − Ta). The rest is the useful gain carried away by the fluid.

Qu = Ac[S − UL(Tp − Ta)] = AcFR[S − UL(Ti − Ta)] = ṁcp(To − Ti); η = Qu/(AcIT)

Definitions and significance (2020 4a, 2021 6a, 2019 4b, 2022 5a, 2023 5a/5b)
TermDefinitionSignificance
Critical radiation level Icthe radiation level at which absorbed energy just equals losses, so useful gain is zero: Ic = UL(Ti − Ta)/(τα)the collector produces useful heat only when IT > Ic; the pump controller should not run below it; Ic rises with operating temperature
Collector efficiency factor F′ratio of the actual useful energy gain to the gain if the whole absorber were at the local fluid temperature; = (1/UL)/(1/Uo), Uo = heat transfer coefficient from fluid to ambientmeasures the quality of the plate-tube design (fin efficiency, bond, hfi); typical 0.8-0.97; constant for a given design
Heat removal factor FRratio of actual useful gain to the gain if the whole absorber were at the fluid inlet temperature: FR = (ṁcp/AcUL)[1 − exp(−AcULF′/ṁcp)] = F′F″lets Qu be computed from the known inlet temperature; like a heat-exchanger effectiveness; rises with flow rate towards F′
Effective (τα)(τα) = τα/[1 − (1 − α)ρd] accounts for multiple reflections between plate and cover; (τα)e ≈ 1.01-1.02(τα) also counts solar energy absorbed in the glass that comes back to the platesets the optical (zero-loss) efficiency FR(τα), the intercept of the efficiency line; selective coatings and low-iron glass raise it
Inclination angle βslope of the collector from the horizontalmaximises incident radiation: β ≈ latitude for year-round use, φ + 10-15° for winter, φ − 10-15° for summer; affects Rb, view of sky/ground and gap convection; thermosiphon/heat pipe need a minimum tilt
Concentration ratio CAa/Ar (see B2)higher C ⇒ smaller lossy receiver ⇒ higher temperature
Losses of a flat plate collector (2023 6a)
  1. Optical losses: reflection at the glass surfaces (~8%), absorption in the glass, dust and shading by the frame, reflection from the absorber (α < 1); grow at large incidence angles.
  2. Top loss (largest thermal loss): natural convection and long-wave radiation from plate to glass, then wind convection and radiation from glass to sky; coefficient Ut.
  3. Bottom (back) loss: conduction through the back insulation and convection/radiation from the casing: Ub ≈ ki/Li.
  4. Edge loss: conduction through the side insulation: Ue = (k/L)edgeAedge/Ac.
  5. Other: heat stored in the collector mass at start-up (heat capacity), pipe and connection losses, night-time reverse circulation.

UL = Ut + Ub + Ue; Ut = [1/(hc,p-c + hr,p-c) + 1/(hw + hr,c-a)]−1

Thermal network for a double-glass-covered FPC (2021 5a)

For two covers the top path has three stages in series: plate Tp → [hc,p-c1 ∥ hr,p-c1] → cover 1 Tc1 → [hc,c1-c2 ∥ hr,c1-c2] → cover 2 Tc2 → [hw ∥ hr,c2-s] → ambient/sky. The bottom path is plate → insulation conduction (L/k) → [hc,b-a ∥ hr,b-a] → ambient, and edge losses in parallel. Absorbed solar S enters at the plate node; Qu leaves to the fluid. So Ut = [1/(hc + hr)p-c1 + 1/(hc + hr)c1-c2 + 1/(hw + hr)c2-a]−1.

Derivation of the collector efficiency factor F′ (2022 5b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Fin of length (W − D)/2 on each side of a tube, thickness δ, conductivity k; absorbed S, loss UL(T − Ta)Each half-plate between tubes is a fin heated by the sun.
Fin equation: d2T/dx2 = (UL/kδ)[T − Ta − S/UL]; m2 = UL/(kδ)Energy balance on a strip dx of the fin.
Heat reaching the tube from both fins: q′fin = (W − D)F[S − UL(Tb − Ta)], F = tanh[m(W − D)/2]/[m(W − D)/2]Standard fin solution (Tb = base temperature at the tube).
Gain over the tube itself: q′tube = D[S − UL(Tb − Ta)] ⇒ q′u = [(W − D)F + D][S − UL(Tb − Ta)]Total per unit length of tube.
Same heat crosses bond and tube wall to the fluid: q′u = (Tb − Tf)/[1/(hfiπDi) + 1/Cb]Cb = bond conductance.
Eliminate Tb between the two equations: q′u = WF′[S − UL(Tf − Ta)]Algebra: solve the second for Tb and substitute.
F′ = (1/UL) / {{W[1/(UL(D + (W − D)F)) + 1/Cb + 1/(πDihfi)]}}Symbols: W tube spacing, D outer and Di inner tube diameter, F fin efficiency, Cb bond conductance, hfi fluid-side coefficient, UL overall loss coefficient.
Testing a new flat plate collector (2022 6a)
  1. Mount the collector outdoors (or in a solar simulator) facing the sun, near normal incidence around solar noon, on a clear day (ASHRAE 93 / ISO 9806).
  2. Circulate fluid at a fixed flow rate (about 0.02 kg/s per m2) with controlled inlet temperature; measure ṁ, Ti, To, irradiance IT (pyranometer in the collector plane), Ta and wind speed.
  3. Record quasi-steady periods (10-15 min) at at least four inlet temperatures from near ambient to high.
  4. For each: η = ṁcp(To − Ti)/(AcIT); plot η against (Ti − Ta)/IT. The straight line gives intercept FR(τα)n and slope −FRUL (Hottel-Whillier-Bliss).
  5. Also measure the time constant (shade and unshade, time to reach 63.2% of the change) and the incidence angle modifier Kτα at several angles; stagnation and pressure/leak tests for durability.
